Q: Ruby block/anonymous function placeholder parameter A:

Ruby does not support Scala style placeholder syntax like f(_), and you cannot implement that exact syntax yourself because Ruby’s parser cannot be extended.

However, Ruby does provide numbered block parameters, which give you a compact way to express the same idea:

[1, 2, 3].map { f(_1) }

If f is a method, you can also pass it directly:

[1, 2, 3].map(&method(:f))

There are currently no plans to add f(_) or similar placeholder syntax to the language.

Q: Spring Boot JPA Bulk insert A:

To enable batch insert you need the batch_size property which you have in your configuration.

Also since a jdbc batch can target one table only you need the spring.jpa.hibernate.order_inserts=true property to order the insert between parent and child or else the statement are unordered and you will see a partial batch (new batch anytime an insert in a different table is called)

Q: In Powershell, is there a way to convert html to a object with depth? A:

You are likely looking for getElementsByTagName

$ret = invoke-webrequest -uri [uri]

$ret.parsedhtml.getelementsbytagname('table')[0]

gets you the first table in your html document

$ret.parsedhtml.getelementsbytagname('tr')[0]

gets you the first <tr> row in your HTML document.

Q: How to set central widget fill in the whole main window in Qt A:

The answers here seem not to understand the basics of Qt containers.

If you place a widget on the QMainWindow in Qt Designer, then view the Object Inspector, click on QMainWindow (the root component in this scenario), then right-click on that, the final item in the context menu is "Layout". Choose "Layout Horizontally" (for example).

The widget under the QMainWindow (which by default will have been set as the central widget of the QMainWindow) will automatically expand to fill the whole of the QMainWindow, including when you resize the QMainWindow.

You can remove the status bar and/or menu if you want: this is completely irrelevant to the question.

Actually by default it won't fill the QMainWindow completely: by default there will be margins around it. These margins in fact belong to the "layout" of the centralwidget: click on that in Object Inspector and then look at the section at the bottom of Property Editor, called "Layout". Change (for example) "layoutLeftMargin" from 9 (default at the time of writing) to 100: you will see that the widget is now permanently positioned 100 pixels to the right of the left edge of the QMainWindow. Again, if you change the size of the QMainWindow, the size of the "central widget" widget will always retain that left margin.

Thus we see that a container determines the type of layout of its child components ... and yet the layout child components also control things like margins for their parent containers. Layouts are themselves "child components".

MRE (using PyQt6):

from PyQt6 import QtWidgets
import sys

app = QtWidgets.QApplication(sys.argv)
mw = QtWidgets.QMainWindow()
mw.resize(800, 600)
centralwidget = QtWidgets.QWidget(parent=mw)
horizontalLayout = QtWidgets.QHBoxLayout(centralwidget)
widget = QtWidgets.QWidget(parent=centralwidget)
widget.setStyleSheet("border: 5px solid red;")
horizontalLayout.addWidget(widget)
margins = horizontalLayout.contentsMargins()
print(f'horizontalLayout margins: bottom {margins.bottom()} left {margins.left()} right {margins.right()} top {margins.top()}')
mw.setCentralWidget(centralwidget)
mw.show()
sys.exit(app.exec())
